query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor addition (1–2 at.%) of Nb to a CoCrFeMnNi-based eutectic high-entropy alloy will enable Nb to segregate at internal lamellar colony boundaries, forming Nb-enriched interfacial complexions that lower boundary energy and create a thin, ductile interphase.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi-based) with dual-phase lamellar colonies exhibiting internal boundaries prone to microcracking under room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Minor alloying addition of 1–2 at.% Nb during melting, followed by a homogenization anneal at ~1100 °C for several hours and a controlled cooling process to promote Nb segregation at the lamellar boundaries.
generation.conditions: Processing must ensure uniform Nb distribution in the melt, an adequate homogenization anneal (approximately 1100 °C for several hours), and controlled cooling to enable Nb segregation specifically to the lamellar colony internal boundaries at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of Nb-enriched interfacial complexions or amorphous intergranular films along the colony boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Nb segregates to the internal boundaries during the heat treatment, reducing boundary energy and facilitating the formation of a ductile interphase. This interphase acts as a barrier that both absorbs local strain and delays crack initiation, while the matrix retains its dislocation-mediated strengthening, leading to improved strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified baseline alloy, the Nb-modified alloy is predicted to exhibit an increased yield strength and enhanced room-temperature tensile ductility due to enhanced boundary cohesion and improved work-hardening, with a corresponding reduction in microcracking under tensile loads.
generation.baseline: Eutectic HEA without Nb addition, characterized by dual-phase lamellar colonies with internal boundaries that are prone to microcrack initiation and propagation under tensile load, leading to brittle failure.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected as long as the Nb addition level is maintained within 1–2 at.% and the processing parameters (annealing temperature, time, and cooling rate) are closely controlled; excessive Nb or inappropriate thermal treatments may lead to the formation of undesired secondary phases.
generation.uncertainty: While the predicted outcomes are supported by the mechanism of boundary segregation and interfacial complexion formation, the exact magnitude of improvements in yield strength and ductility, and the sensitivity to processing parameters, remain uncertain until experimentally quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeMnNi-based eutectic HEA samples, one with 1–2 at.% Nb addition and one without. Subject both sets to identical homogenization annealing at 1100 °C and controlled cooling. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests and microscopy (e.g., TEM, atom probe tomography) to examine the internal boundary chemistry and microstructure.
measurements: Room-temperature yield strength and tensile ductility (total elongation)
Microcrack density near internal lamellar boundaries via SEM/TEM
Characterization of Nb segregation at boundaries using atom probe or EDS mapping
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-added samples do not show statistically significant improvements in both yield strength and ductility relative to the baseline, or if microscopy fails to reveal Nb enrichment and the formation of an interfacial ductile phase at the internal boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.

proposals.material_system: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi-based HEA) with dual-phase lamellar colonies
proposals.intervention: Minor alloying addition of a boundary‐segregating element (e.g., Nb)
proposals.conditions: Add 1–2 at.% Nb during melting, followed by a homogenization anneal at ~1100 °C for several hours and controlled cooling to promote Nb segregation at internal lamellar boundaries at room temperature
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation of Nb-enriched interfacial complexions or amorphous intergranular films along the colony boundaries
proposals.mechanism: Nb segregation modifies the chemistry at the internal boundaries, lowering boundary energy and creating a thin, ductile interphase that can absorb strain and delay crack initiation while retaining or even increasing dislocation-mediated strengthening within the lamellae
proposals.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified baseline, the alloy is expected to exhibit an enhanced combination of yield strength and tensile ductility at room temperature due to increased boundary cohesion and improved work-hardening, with reduced microcracking under tensile load
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This single chemical intervention directly targets the microstructural weak points (internal lamellar boundaries) responsible for crack initiation by creating ductile boundary films, thereby simultaneously enhancing strength and ductility without altering the dual-phase nature of the alloy

proposals.material_system: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy with lamellar colonies (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi system)
proposals.conditions: Apply FSP with optimized tool rotational speeds (e.g., 800–1200 rpm) and traverse rates on the as-cast alloy at ambient temperature, ensuring adequate stirring without overheating to avoid dissolving the lamellar morphology
proposals.structural_mediator: Refinement of the lamellar spacing and enhanced continuity of internal boundaries
proposals.mechanism: FSP introduces significant plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization localized within the near-surface region, leading to a homogenized and refined dual-phase lamellar structure where boundaries are less susceptible to cracking. The refined microstructure increases the density of barriers to dislocation motion (strengthening) and improves ductile strain accommodation at the refined boundaries
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, the friction stir processed alloy is predicted to show increased yield and ultimate strengths along with improved tensile ductility, as the refined microstructure delays crack initiation and propagation during deformation
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By mechanically refining the microstructure in situ, this intervention alleviates the trade-off between strength and ductility, specifically targeting the microcrack-prone interfaces without compromising the underlying dual-phase lamellar architecture

proposals.material_system: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy (e.g., CoCuFeMnNi system) with well-defined lamellar colonies
proposals.conditions: Use a high-power laser to locally melt the alloy surface under a controlled atmosphere, followed by rapid quenching (cooling rates on the order of 10^4–10^6 K/s) to re-solidify the lamellar structure
proposals.structural_mediator: Reduction of lamellar spacing and development of favorable residual stress states at the phase boundaries
proposals.mechanism: The rapid solidification induced by laser remelting results in finer lamellae and introduces beneficial residual compressive stresses at the internal boundaries. The smaller lamellar spacing improves dislocation interactions (increasing strength) while the residual stresses help to mitigate crack initiation and propagation (improving ductility)
proposals.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified baseline, the laser-remelted alloy should display simultaneously higher tensile strength and improved ductility at room temperature owing to microstructural refinement and stress state optimization
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This processing route represents a single, controllable thermal intervention that refines the critical features of the microstructure (lamellar spacing and internal stresses) which govern both strength and ductility during room-temperature deformation

proposals.material_system: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi)
proposals.intervention: Application of a thin, diffusion-enabled interfacial ceramic nanocoating
proposals.conditions: Deposit a uniform ~10–20 nm layer of Al2O3 via atomic layer deposition (ALD) onto the as-cast alloy, followed by a brief annealing treatment (~800 °C for 10–30 minutes) in an inert atmosphere to promote partial diffusion along the internal boundaries
proposals.structural_mediator: Strengthening of the interlamellar interfaces by formation of a robust, nanolayered ceramic interphase at colony boundaries
proposals.mechanism: The ultrathin ceramic coating diffuses along the internal boundaries during annealing and forms a well-bonded interfacial layer that bridges the dual-phase interface. This layer acts as a barrier against microcrack initiation and propagation, while still permitting dislocation transfer and work hardening, thereby enhancing both strength and ductility
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated lamellar baseline, the coated and annealed alloy is expected to show increased room-temperature tensile strength along with an enhanced ductility, as the engineered interfacial layer effectively delays crack growth and enables better energy absorption during deformation
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This surface/coating intervention directly modifies the most vulnerable regions (internal boundaries) without altering the bulk dual-phase structure, providing a single-step route to overcome the intrinsic brittleness of conventional eutectic high-entropy alloys

decision.rationale: Direction A is chosen because its minor alloying addition of Nb directly targets the problematic internal lamellar boundaries by promoting Nb segregation. This segregation is expected to form an interfacial complexion that both absorbs strain and delays crack initiation while maintaining or enhancing dislocation-mediated strengthening. The intervention modifies the chemistry at the boundaries without altering the dual-phase lamellar architecture. Its clear mechanism and straightforward processing conditions make it a promising single intervention for simultaneously improving strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
